title: Login to Azure
description: Authenticate to Azure and list accessible subscriptions — opens a browser for interactive login, with flags for service principal or device-code flows.

breakdown.meaning: Azure CLI entry point
Authenticate and store credentials for subsequent az commands

flags.description: Authenticate as a service principal (for CI/CD pipelines)
Service principal app ID or user UPN
Service principal client secret or certificate path
Azure AD tenant ID to authenticate against
Device code flow — for headless environments without a browser

example: az login --service-principal --username $APP_ID --password $CLIENT_SECRET --tenant $TENANT_ID
tip: Use --use-device-code in SSH sessions or CI environments without a browser. For CI/CD pipelines, authenticate with a service principal and store APP_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, and TENANT_ID as environment variables — never hardcode them in scripts.

title: List subscriptions
description: Show all Azure subscriptions accessible to the current account, with their names, IDs, and which is currently active.

breakdown.meaning: List all subscriptions accessible with current credentials
Render output as an ASCII table

flags.description: Output format — table for human review, json for scripting
Include disabled subscriptions in the list
Fetch fresh subscription data from Azure instead of cached info
JMESPath expression to filter or reshape output

example: az account list --query '[].{Name:name, ID:id, State:state}' --output table
tip: Run with --refresh after login to ensure the list reflects the latest subscription access. Use 'az account show' to confirm which subscription is currently active before running any resource commands.

title: Switch active subscription
description: Set the active Azure subscription for all subsequent commands — persisted to the CLI profile until changed or overridden per-command.

breakdown.meaning: Change the active subscription for the CLI session
Target subscription by name or GUID

flags.description: Subscription name or ID to activate

example: az account set --subscription 12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012 && az account show --query name -o tsv
tip: Use the subscription GUID rather than the name in scripts — display names can change or be duplicated across tenants. Always follow with 'az account show' to verify the correct subscription is active before running destructive commands.

title: List resource groups
description: Show all resource groups in the active subscription with their names, locations, and provisioning state.

breakdown.meaning: List all resource groups in the current subscription
Render as an ASCII table

flags.description: Output format
JMESPath expression to filter results
Filter groups by a specific tag

example: az group list --query '[?location==`eastus`].{Name:name, State:properties.provisioningState}' --output table
output:
Name              Location    ProvisioningState
----------------  ----------  -----------------
prod-rg           eastus      Succeeded
dev-rg            westeurope  Succeeded
staging-rg        eastus      Succeeded
tip: Filter by location with '--query "[?location=='eastus']"'. Use 'az group show -n rg-name' for a specific group including full tag details. Delete a group and all its resources at once with 'az group delete -n my-rg --yes --no-wait'.

title: Create resource group
description: Create a new resource group in a specified Azure region — all related resources for a project should share a group for unified management, RBAC, and cleanup.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new resource group
Name of the resource group — use a consistent naming convention
Azure region where the group's metadata is stored

flags.description: Resource group name
Azure region (e.g. eastus, westeurope, australiaeast)
Tags for cost allocation and policy enforcement

example: az group create --name my-app-rg --location eastus --tags env=prod team=platform cost-center=eng
tip: Add tags at creation time for cost allocation and policy enforcement — they're much harder to add consistently after resources exist. Resources inherit the group's location by default but can be in a different region.

title: List virtual machines
description: Show all VMs in a resource group or across the subscription with their power state, size, OS, and public IP addresses.

breakdown.meaning: List virtual machines in the subscription or a resource group
Scope to a specific resource group — omit to list all VMs in the subscription
Include power state and public IPs — requires an extra API call per VM
Render as an ASCII table

flags.description: Limit to VMs in this resource group
Include VM power state and network details (slower)
JMESPath filter expression

example: az vm list --show-details --query '[].{Name:name, State:powerState, Size:hardwareProfile.vmSize}' --output table
output:
Name       PowerState   Size           PublicIps
---------  -----------  -------------  ---------------
web-vm-1   VM running   Standard_D2s   40.112.128.10
db-vm-1    VM running   Standard_D4s
web-vm-2   VM stopped   Standard_D2s
tip: Use --show-details to include power state and public IPs in one call — without it you need a separate 'az vm show' per instance. Omit --resource-group to list all VMs across the subscription, but expect a slower response.

title: Start a virtual machine
description: Start a stopped or deallocated Azure VM — compute billing resumes and the VM gets a new public IP unless a static IP is assigned.

breakdown.meaning: Power on a stopped or deallocated virtual machine
Resource group containing the VM
Name of the virtual machine to start

flags.description: Resource group of the VM
Virtual machine name
Return immediately without waiting for the VM to finish starting

example: az vm start --resource-group my-rg --name my-vm --no-wait && az vm wait --resource-group my-rg --name my-vm --running
tip: Use --no-wait to start asynchronously and continue script execution. Follow with 'az vm wait --running' to block until the VM is fully running. Assign a static public IP to prevent the address changing after each stop/start cycle.

title: Deallocate VM (stop billing)
description: Deallocate a VM to stop compute billing — unlike 'az vm stop', deallocate releases the underlying hardware and stops the compute charge completely.

breakdown.meaning: Shut down the VM and release its compute resources to stop billing
Resource group containing the VM
Virtual machine name to deallocate

flags.description: Resource group of the VM
Virtual machine name
Return immediately without waiting for deallocation to complete

example: az vm deallocate --resource-group my-rg --name my-vm --no-wait
tip: Always use 'deallocate' rather than 'az vm stop' — 'az vm stop' shuts the OS down but keeps the VM allocated, so compute costs continue. Disk storage costs still apply when deallocated, but at a fraction of running costs.

command: az storage blob upload --account-name mystorageaccount --container-name mycontainer --name myfile.txt --file ./myfile.txt --auth-mode login
title: Upload blob to storage
description: Upload a local file to Azure Blob Storage in a specified container — supports large files, custom metadata, content types, and access tier selection.

breakdown.meaning: Upload a single file to a blob container
Storage account name
Target blob container
Blob name (path) in the container
Local source file to upload
Authenticate using current Azure CLI login instead of a storage key

flags.description: Use Azure AD credentials instead of storage account keys
Set the access tier for cost optimisation
Set MIME type (e.g. application/json)
Upload an entire directory to the container

example: az storage blob upload-batch --account-name mysa --destination mycontainer --source ./dist --auth-mode login
tip: Prefer --auth-mode login over storage account keys to avoid managing long-lived credentials. Use 'upload-batch' to upload entire directories. Set --tier Archive for infrequently accessed data to reduce storage costs by ~90%.

title: Configure kubectl for AKS
description: Merge the kubeconfig for an AKS cluster into ~/.kube/config, enabling kubectl commands authenticated via Azure AD credentials.

breakdown.meaning: Fetch AKS cluster credentials and merge into local kubeconfig
Resource group containing the AKS cluster
AKS cluster name

flags.description: Resource group of the cluster
AKS cluster name
Overwrite existing context with the same name
Set a custom context name instead of the cluster name
Get admin kubeconfig — bypasses AAD auth, use sparingly

example: az aks get-credentials --resource-group prod-rg --name prod-cluster --overwrite-existing --context prod-aks
tip: Use --context prod-aks to set a short, memorable context name instead of the cluster name. Use --overwrite-existing in CI pipelines to prevent the command from failing if the context already exists.

title: Login to container registry
description: Authenticate Docker to push and pull images from Azure Container Registry using current Azure credentials — token is valid for 3 hours.

breakdown.meaning: Authenticate Docker to an Azure Container Registry
ACR registry name (without .azurecr.io suffix)

flags.description: Container registry name
Return the raw token instead of logging Docker in — for environments without Docker
Specify the resource group if the registry name is ambiguous

example: az acr login --name myregistry && docker push myregistry.azurecr.io/myapp:latest
tip: The ACR hostname format is registryname.azurecr.io. Use --expose-token for environments running containerd or Podman instead of Docker. Enable 'Admin user' on the registry only as a fallback — prefer service principal auth in CI pipelines.

title: List App Service apps
description: Show all App Service web apps in a resource group with their names, state, location, and default hostname.

breakdown.meaning: List all App Service web apps in the subscription or resource group
Scope the list to a specific resource group
Render as ASCII table

flags.description: Filter by resource group
JMESPath expression to extract specific fields
Stream live application logs from App Service

example: az webapp list --query '[].{Name:name, State:state, URL:defaultHostName}' --output table
output:
Name            State    URL
--------------  -------  ---------------------------------
my-web-app      Running  my-web-app.azurewebsites.net
my-api-app      Running  my-api-app.azurewebsites.net
my-staging      Stopped  my-staging.azurewebsites.net
tip: Use 'az webapp log tail -n myapp -g myrg' to stream live application logs. Deploy a ZIP package with 'az webapp deployment source config-zip -g myrg -n myapp --src app.zip' — no full CI pipeline required for quick deployments.

command: az keyvault secret show --vault-name my-vault --name db-password
title: Read Key Vault secret
description: Retrieve a secret value from Azure Key Vault — returns the secret string along with version ID, expiry date, and enabled status.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve the current value and metadata for a Key Vault secret
Name of the Key Vault
Secret name within the vault

flags.description: Key Vault name
Secret name
Retrieve a specific version of the secret
Extract just the secret value field

example: az keyvault secret show --vault-name my-vault --name db-password --query value --output tsv
tip: Use '--query value --output tsv' to extract just the secret value for scripting. In App Service and Functions, reference secrets directly with Key Vault references (@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)) in app settings — eliminates runtime CLI calls entirely.

command: az network vnet list --resource-group my-rg --output table
title: List virtual networks
description: Show all virtual networks in a resource group with their address spaces and subnet counts — starting point for diagnosing connectivity and peering issues.

breakdown.meaning: List virtual networks in the subscription or a resource group
Scope to a specific resource group
Render as ASCII table

flags.description: Filter to a specific resource group
JMESPath to extract address spaces or subnet names
Get full details of a specific VNet including subnets and peerings

example: az network vnet show --resource-group my-rg --name my-vnet --query '{Name:name, Space:addressSpace.addressPrefixes, Subnets:subnets[*].name}'
output:
Name      Location  AddressSpace   NumSubnets
--------  --------  -------------  ----------
my-vnet   eastus    10.0.0.0/16    3
prod-net  eastus    172.16.0.0/12  5
tip: Use 'az network vnet show' with --query to inspect subnet CIDR ranges, NSG associations, and service endpoints. Use 'az network vnet peering list --vnet-name myvnet -g myrg' to check VNet-to-VNet connections and their sync state.

command: az role assignment list --assignee user@example.com --output table
title: List RBAC role assignments
description: Show all Azure RBAC role assignments for a user, service principal, or group — essential for auditing access and troubleshooting permission denied errors.

breakdown.meaning: List role assignments at subscription, resource group, or resource scope
Filter to assignments for a specific user, service principal, or group by UPN or object ID
Render as ASCII table

flags.description: Filter by user, service principal, or group
Limit to a specific resource scope
Limit to resource group scope
Include all assignments in the subscription, not just the current scope
Show assignments inherited from parent scopes

example: az role assignment list --assignee user@example.com --all --include-inherited --output table
output:
Principal             Role          Scope
--------------------  ------------  ----------------------------------
user@example.com      Contributor   /subscriptions/12345678...
user@example.com      Reader        /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/prod-rg
tip: Use --all --include-inherited to see the full effective permission set, not just direct assignments at the current scope. Use 'az role definition list --name Contributor --output json' to see what actions a given role actually permits.

command: az monitor log-analytics query --workspace my-workspace-id --analytics-query 'AzureActivity | limit 20'
title: Query Log Analytics
description: Run a KQL (Kusto Query Language) query against a Log Analytics workspace to search logs and metrics from Azure services.

breakdown.meaning: Execute a KQL query against a Log Analytics workspace
Log Analytics workspace ID (a GUID, not the workspace name)
KQL query string — pipe-based syntax similar to bash

flags.description: Workspace customer ID (GUID) — find with 'az monitor log-analytics workspace show --query customerId'
KQL query string
ISO 8601 duration (e.g. P1D = last 24h, PT1H = last hour)

example: az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $(az monitor log-analytics workspace show -n myws -g myrg --query customerId -o tsv) --analytics-query 'ContainerLog | where LogEntry contains "ERROR" | limit 50' --timespan PT1H
tip: The --workspace value must be the workspace GUID (customerId), not its display name — use the subshell pattern in the example to look it up automatically. Use --timespan P1D for last 24 hours (ISO 8601 duration format).

command: az container create --resource-group my-rg --name my-container --image nginx:latest --ports 80 --dns-name-label my-app
title: Run a container (ACI)
description: Deploy a Docker container using Azure Container Instances — serverless container hosting billed per second, no cluster management required.

breakdown.meaning: Create and start a container group in Azure Container Instances
Resource group to deploy the container into
Container group name
Docker image to run
Ports to expose publicly
DNS label — container is reachable at my-app.region.azurecontainer.io

flags.description: Docker image (public or from ACR)
Ports to expose
CPU cores to allocate (e.g. 1, 2)
Memory in GB to allocate
Environment variables passed to the container
Private registry hostname (for ACR images)

example: az container create --resource-group my-rg --name my-job --image myregistry.azurecr.io/processor:latest --registry-login-server myregistry.azurecr.io --cpu 2 --memory 4 --restart-policy Never
tip: ACI is ideal for short-lived batch jobs and one-off tasks — no cluster overhead, billed per second. Use --restart-policy Never for batch jobs that should not restart. Use 'az container logs -n my-container -g my-rg' for output and 'az container delete' to stop billing.

title: List Function Apps
description: Show all Azure Function Apps in a resource group with their state, location, and runtime — the starting point for managing and deploying serverless functions.

breakdown.meaning: List Azure Function Apps in the subscription or resource group
Scope to a specific resource group
Render as ASCII table

flags.description: Filter to a specific resource group
JMESPath expression to extract specific fields
Show full details including runtime stack and app settings keys

example: az functionapp show --resource-group my-rg --name my-func --query '{Name:name, State:state, Runtime:siteConfig.linuxFxVersion}'
output:
Name              State    Location    Kind
----------------  -------  ----------  --------
my-func-app       Running  East US     functionapp
data-processor    Running  East US     functionapp
tip: Deploy a ZIP package with 'az functionapp deployment source config-zip -g myrg -n myfunc --src func.zip'. Stream live logs with 'az webapp log tail -n myfunc -g myrg'. Check runtime version with 'az functionapp show --query siteConfig.linuxFxVersion'.

command: az ad user create --display-name "Jane Doe" --user-principal-name jane@contoso.com --password TempP@ss1 --force-change-password-next-sign-in true
title: Create Azure AD user
description: Create a new user account in Azure Active Directory with a temporary password that must be changed on first login — used for onboarding employees or service accounts.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new user object in Azure AD (Entra ID)
Full display name shown in the directory and email clients
UPN — the login email address for the user
Initial password; must meet the tenant password policy
Require password reset on first login — best practice for onboarding

example: az ad user create --display-name "Jane Doe" --user-principal-name jane@contoso.com --password "TempP@ss$(date +%Y)!" --force-change-password-next-sign-in true --mail-nickname jane
tip: Always set --force-change-password-next-sign-in true when creating accounts so the temp password is never the long-term credential. Prefer automating bulk user creation from CSV with a loop over this command rather than using the portal, which does not scale.

command: az ad user list --output table --query "[].{Name:displayName, UPN:userPrincipalName, Enabled:accountEnabled}"
title: List Azure AD users
description: Retrieve all user accounts from Azure Active Directory with their display names, login UPNs, and enabled state — useful for audits and bulk operations.

breakdown.meaning: List all users in the Azure AD tenant
Format the result as a human-readable ASCII table
JMESPath projection to show only the three most relevant fields

example: az ad user list --filter "accountEnabled eq true" --query "[].{Name:displayName, UPN:userPrincipalName}" --output table
output:
Name          UPN                       Enabled
------------  ------------------------  -------
Jane Doe      jane@contoso.com          True
John Smith    john@contoso.com          True
Old Account   former@contoso.com        False
tip: Use --filter with OData syntax (e.g. "accountEnabled eq true" or "startswith(displayName,'A')") to reduce API response size. Large tenants can return thousands of users; always filter in CI scripts to avoid token-size errors and slow queries.

title: Delete Azure AD user
description: Permanently delete a user account from Azure Active Directory — removes sign-in access immediately and the account lands in the 30-day soft-delete recycle bin.

breakdown.meaning: Delete a user from Azure AD (soft-delete, recoverable for 30 days)
Identify the user by UPN, object ID, or email address

example: az ad user delete --id $(az ad user show --id jane@contoso.com --query id --output tsv)
tip: Deletion is soft — the user lands in the AAD recycle bin for 30 days and can be restored with "az ad user restore --id OBJECT_ID". Revoke active tokens immediately after deletion by also running "az ad user revoke-sign-in-sessions --id UPN" to terminate live sessions.

command: az ad user update --id jane@contoso.com --display-name "Jane A. Doe" --account-enabled true
title: Update Azure AD user
description: Modify attributes of an existing Azure AD user account — change display names, enable or disable accounts, set department, or force a password reset.

breakdown.meaning: Update attributes of an existing Azure AD user object
Target user identified by UPN or object ID
New display name to set for the account
Re-enable a previously disabled account (or set false to disable)

example: az ad user update --id jane@contoso.com --account-enabled false --force-change-password-next-sign-in true
tip: To disable a user without deleting (e.g. a leaver who may return), set --account-enabled false — this blocks login instantly without losing group memberships or license assignments. Pair with --force-change-password-next-sign-in true when handing over accounts.

command: az ad group create --display-name "Platform Engineers" --mail-nickname platform-engineers
title: Create Azure AD group
description: Create a security group in Azure AD to manage access collectively — assign RBAC roles or application permissions to the group instead of individual users.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new security or Microsoft 365 group in Azure AD
Human-readable group name shown in the portal and IAM views
Short alias used for the group email address and internal identifier

example: az ad group create --display-name "Platform Engineers" --mail-nickname platform-engineers --description "Team responsible for shared infrastructure"
tip: Assign RBAC roles to groups rather than individual users — when someone joins or leaves the team you only update group membership, not every resource role assignment. Use the returned group object ID when running "az role assignment create --assignee-object-id".

command: az ad group member add --group "Platform Engineers" --member-id <user-object-id>
title: Add member to Azure AD group
description: Add a user, service principal, or nested group to an Azure AD security group — the member inherits all RBAC and app roles assigned to the group immediately.

breakdown.meaning: Add a member (user, SP, or group) to an Azure AD group
Target group identified by display name or object ID
Object ID of the user, service principal, or nested group to add

example: USER_OID=$(az ad user show --id jane@contoso.com --query id --output tsv) && az ad group member add --group "Platform Engineers" --member-id "$USER_OID"
tip: The --member-id must be an Azure AD object ID, not a UPN or email — use "az ad user show --id UPN --query id -o tsv" to resolve it first. Check current membership with "az ad group member list --group GROUP_NAME --output table" before adding to avoid duplicates.

command: az ad sp create-for-rbac --name my-cicd-sp --role Contributor --scopes /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/my-rg
title: Create service principal for automation
description: Create an Azure AD service principal with a client secret and assign it an RBAC role — the standard way to grant non-human identities (CI/CD pipelines, scripts) access to Azure resources.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new app registration and service principal together with a client secret
Display name for the service principal in the Azure AD app list
Built-in RBAC role to assign — use the minimum required role (Reader, Contributor, or custom)
Resource scope for the role assignment — prefer resource group over full subscription

example: az ad sp create-for-rbac --name my-cicd-sp --role Contributor --scopes /subscriptions/$SUB_ID/resourceGroups/my-rg --sdk-auth
tip: Scope the role assignment to a resource group rather than the whole subscription to limit blast radius. The generated client secret expires — set a calendar reminder to rotate it before expiry with "az ad sp credential reset --id APP_ID". Store the output JSON as a CI/CD secret, not in code.

title: List all resources in a group
description: Show every Azure resource in a resource group or subscription regardless of type — a fast way to inventory what exists before making changes or estimating costs.

breakdown.meaning: List resources across all types in the active subscription or a resource group
Scope the listing to a single resource group — omit to search the whole subscription
Render as ASCII table with Name, ResourceGroup, Location, Type columns

example: az resource list --resource-group my-rg --query "[].{Name:name, Type:type, Location:location}" --output table
output:
Name              Type                                    Location
----------------  --------------------------------------  --------
my-vm             Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines       eastus
my-vnet           Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks       eastus
my-storage        Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts       eastus
tip: Filter by resource type with "--resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines" to narrow results. Use "--tag env=prod" to list only tagged resources — essential for cost tracking. Combine with "az resource delete" for bulk cleanup of non-prod environments.

title: Delete a resource by ID
description: Delete any Azure resource by its full resource ID — useful for bulk cleanup via scripted loops or when the resource-type-specific subcommand is not available.

breakdown.meaning: Delete an Azure resource using its full ARM resource ID
One or more full resource IDs (space-separated); get IDs from "az resource list --query [].id"
Print detailed request/response info — useful for diagnosing failed deletions

example: az resource list --resource-group old-rg --query "[].id" --output tsv | xargs az resource delete --ids
tip: Pass multiple IDs to --ids in a single call to batch-delete — more efficient than looping. For whole environments, "az group delete -n rg-name --yes --no-wait" deletes the group and all contained resources in one command and is generally faster than individual resource deletions.

command: az deployment group create --resource-group my-rg --template-file azuredeploy.json --parameters @azuredeploy.parameters.json
title: Deploy ARM template
description: Deploy an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to a resource group — the native infrastructure-as-code mechanism for provisioning any Azure resource declaratively.

breakdown.meaning: Start an ARM template deployment scoped to a resource group
Target resource group for the deployment
Path to the ARM template JSON file (or Bicep file if Bicep CLI is installed)
Parameter file prefixed with @ to pass values into the template; can also pass inline KEY=VALUE pairs

example: az deployment group create --resource-group my-rg --template-file main.bicep --parameters env=prod location=eastus --what-if
tip: Add --what-if to preview resource changes before deploying — equivalent to Terraform plan. Use --mode Complete only when you intend to delete resources not defined in the template; default mode is Incremental, which is safer. Bicep files are compiled automatically when passed to --template-file if the Bicep CLI is installed.

command: az storage account create --name mystorageacct --resource-group my-rg --location eastus --sku Standard_LRS --kind StorageV2
title: Create storage account
description: Provision a new Azure Storage account that can host blobs, queues, tables, and file shares — select the replication SKU based on durability requirements and cost budget.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new Azure Storage account in a resource group
Storage account name — globally unique, 3-24 lowercase alphanumeric characters
Resource group to place the account in
Azure region for the primary storage endpoint
Replication type: LRS=local, ZRS=zone, GRS=geo, RAGRS=read-access geo
Account kind — StorageV2 is recommended for all new accounts; supports all features

example: az storage account create --name mystorageacct --resource-group my-rg --location eastus --sku Standard_GRS --kind StorageV2 --allow-blob-public-access false --min-tls-version TLS1_2
tip: Set --allow-blob-public-access false and --min-tls-version TLS1_2 at creation time to harden the account by default — these are not the defaults in all regions. Use Standard_GRS or Standard_RAGRS for production data that requires geo-redundancy and SLA guarantees.

command: az network nsg rule create --resource-group my-rg --nsg-name my-nsg --name AllowHTTPS --priority 100 --protocol Tcp --destination-port-ranges 443 --access Allow --direction Inbound
title: Add NSG inbound rule
description: Add an inbound security rule to an Azure Network Security Group — controls which traffic is allowed into a subnet or network interface on a specific port and protocol.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new rule inside an existing Network Security Group
Resource group containing the NSG
Name of the NSG to modify
Descriptive rule name — use a convention like Allow/Deny + Protocol + Port
Rule evaluation order — lower numbers are processed first (100–4096); must be unique per NSG
Network protocol: Tcp, Udp, or * (any)
Port(s) to allow or deny; use ranges like 8000-8080 or * for any
Action: Allow or Deny traffic matching this rule
Traffic direction: Inbound (incoming to resource) or Outbound

example: az network nsg rule create --resource-group my-rg --nsg-name my-nsg --name AllowSSHFromCorp --priority 200 --protocol Tcp --source-address-prefixes 10.0.0.0/8 --destination-port-ranges 22 --access Allow --direction Inbound
tip: Restrict --source-address-prefixes to known IP ranges rather than * (any) — especially for SSH (22) and RDP (3389). Use priority gaps (100, 200, 300) rather than consecutive numbers so you can insert rules later without renumbering. View effective rules with "az network nic show-effective-nsg -n NIC -g RG".

command: az lock create --name no-delete --resource-group my-rg --lock-type CanNotDelete
title: Create resource lock
description: Apply a management lock to a resource group or individual resource to prevent accidental deletion or modification — even subscription owners cannot bypass locks without removing them first.

breakdown.meaning: Create an Azure management lock on a subscription, resource group, or individual resource
Lock name — descriptive so teams understand its purpose
Apply the lock to the entire resource group and all resources within it
Lock type: CanNotDelete (read and modify allowed, delete blocked) or ReadOnly (all changes blocked)

example: az lock create --name protect-prod-db --resource-group prod-rg --resource-name prod-sql --resource-type Microsoft.Sql/servers --lock-type CanNotDelete --notes "Contact DBA team before removing"
tip: Use CanNotDelete for production databases and storage accounts to prevent accidental destruction in runbook mistakes. ReadOnly is stricter — it also blocks writes, which can break services that need to update resource metadata. List all locks with "az lock list --resource-group my-rg" before deleting resources.

title: Connect to Azure (PowerShell)
description: Authenticate to Azure using the Az PowerShell module — opens an interactive browser login, with support for service principal and managed identity auth for automation.

breakdown.meaning: Authenticate and establish an Azure session for all subsequent Az cmdlets
Azure AD tenant ID — required when your account has access to multiple tenants
Set the active subscription immediately after login

example: Connect-AzAccount -ServicePrincipal -TenantId $env:AZURE_TENANT_ID -Credential (New-Object PSCredential $env:AZURE_CLIENT_ID, (ConvertTo-SecureString $env:AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET -AsPlainText -Force))
output:
Account                   SubscriptionName   TenantId
-------                   ----------------   --------
user@contoso.com          Prod Subscription  87654321-...
tip: For unattended scripts, authenticate with a service principal using -ServicePrincipal and -Credential rather than interactive browser login. In Azure VMs or App Service, use Connect-AzAccount -Identity to authenticate with a managed identity — no credentials to store or rotate.

title: Get / Set Azure context (PowerShell)
description: Display the current Azure subscription and account context in the PowerShell session, or switch to a different subscription using Set-AzContext.

breakdown.meaning: Show the active tenant, subscription, and account identity for the current PowerShell session

example:
Get-AzContext | Select-Object Name, Account, Subscription
Set-AzContext -SubscriptionId "12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012"
tip: Always run Get-AzContext at the start of automation scripts to assert the correct subscription is active before making changes. Use Set-AzContext -SubscriptionId to switch without re-authenticating. Save and restore context with Save-AzContext / Import-AzContext for parallel pipeline jobs that need different subscription scopes.

command: Get-AzResource -ResourceGroupName my-rg | Select-Object Name, ResourceType, Location | Format-Table
title: List resources (PowerShell)
description: Retrieve all Azure resources in a subscription or resource group using PowerShell — pipe the output to Where-Object or Select-Object to filter and shape results for automation.

breakdown.meaning: List all Azure resources accessible under the current context
Scope the query to a specific resource group — omit to search all groups in the subscription
Project only the three most useful properties
Render as a formatted table in the console

example: Get-AzResource -ResourceGroupName my-rg | Where-Object { $_.ResourceType -eq "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines" }
output:
Name       ResourceType                            Location
----       ------------                            --------
my-vm      Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines       eastus
my-vnet    Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks       eastus
tip: Filter early with -ResourceType "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines" to avoid fetching all resource types when you only care about one. The objects returned are full ARM resource descriptors — pipe to Get-AzResource -ResourceId $_.ResourceId for deeper property inspection without a second cmdlet call.

title: Create resource group (PowerShell)
description: Create a new Azure resource group in a specified region using PowerShell — the logical container for all related resources in a project or environment.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new resource group in the active subscription
Name for the resource group — use a naming convention like {project}-{env}-rg
Azure region where group metadata is stored (resources can be in any region)
Key-value tag pairs as a PowerShell hashtable — used for cost allocation and policy enforcement

example: New-AzResourceGroup -Name my-app-rg -Location eastus -Tag @{env="prod"; team="platform"; "cost-center"="eng-001"}
output:
ResourceGroupName : my-app-rg
Location          : eastus
ProvisioningState : Succeeded
Tags              : {env=prod, team=platform}
tip: Tag resource groups at creation with cost-center, environment, and owner tags — Azure Cost Management uses these tags for billing breakdowns. The -Force parameter suppresses the confirmation prompt for use in scripts. Check if a group already exists before creating with "Get-AzResourceGroup -Name my-rg -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue".

title: Delete resource group (PowerShell)
description: Delete an Azure resource group and all resources it contains — cascades deletion to every VM, disk, VNet, and storage account within the group permanently.

breakdown.meaning: Delete a resource group and all resources contained within it
Name of the resource group to delete
Skip the interactive confirmation prompt — required in unattended scripts

example: Remove-AzResourceGroup -Name dev-temp-rg -Force -AsJob
tip: Add -AsJob to run the deletion asynchronously and continue script execution — useful when deleting large groups. Check for management locks first with "Get-AzResourceLock -ResourceGroupName my-rg" — the deletion will fail silently if a lock is in place. This operation is irreversible; prefer deleting dev/test groups rather than production.

title: List VMs (PowerShell)
description: Retrieve virtual machine objects from Azure using PowerShell — returns full VM descriptors that can be piped into Start-AzVM, Stop-AzVM, or property-access expressions.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve one or all VM objects in the subscription or resource group
Scope to a specific resource group — omit for all VMs in the subscription
Project VM name, region, and SKU size using a calculated property

example: Get-AzVM -ResourceGroupName my-rg -Status | Where-Object { $_.PowerState -ne "VM running" } | Select-Object Name, PowerState
output:
Name       Location  Size
----       --------  ----
web-vm-1   eastus    Standard_D2s_v3
db-vm-1    eastus    Standard_D4s_v3
tip: Add -Status to include VM power state (running/deallocated/stopped) — without it the PowerState property is null. Pipe to Start-AzVM or Stop-AzVM to act on filtered results in a single pipeline. Use Get-AzVM -Name specific-vm -ResourceGroupName rg to get the full ARM object for a single VM.

title: Get Azure AD user (PowerShell)
description: Retrieve an Azure AD user object by UPN or display name — returns the object ID, account enabled state, and assigned licenses needed for downstream automation.

breakdown.meaning: Query Azure AD for user objects using the Az PowerShell module
Filter to a specific user by their login UPN; alternatively use -DisplayName or -ObjectId

example: Get-AzADUser -StartsWith "jane" | Select-Object DisplayName, UserPrincipalName, Id, AccountEnabled
output:
DisplayName  UserPrincipalName      Id                                    AccountEnabled
-----------  -----------------      --                                    --------------
Jane Doe     jane@contoso.com       aaaa1111-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeffffgggg  True
tip: Use -StartsWith for prefix-based searches across large tenants without pulling the full user list. The Id property (object ID) returned here is what you pass to New-AzRoleAssignment -ObjectId or Add-AzADGroupMember -MemberObjectId for downstream RBAC operations.

title: Create Azure AD user (PowerShell)
description: Create a new user account in Azure AD from PowerShell — integrates naturally with PowerShell pipelines for bulk onboarding workflows that read from CSV or HR system exports.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new user object in Azure Active Directory via the Az module
Full name shown in the portal and email clients
Login UPN (email) for the new account
Initial password as a SecureString — never pass plain text passwords directly in scripts
Short alias used for the email address — required field

example: Import-Csv users.csv | ForEach-Object { New-AzADUser -DisplayName $_.Name -UserPrincipalName $_.UPN -Password (ConvertTo-SecureString $_.TempPass -AsPlainText -Force) -MailNickname $_.Alias -ForceChangePasswordNextLogin }
output:
DisplayName  UserPrincipalName   Id
-----------  -----------------   --
Jane Doe     jane@contoso.com    aaaa1111-...
tip: For bulk onboarding, pipe Import-Csv directly into New-AzADUser as shown in the example — far more efficient than manual portal entry. Always use -ForceChangePasswordNextLogin to force a password reset on first sign-in. Store temp passwords in a secret manager rather than in the CSV file itself.

title: Remove Azure AD user (PowerShell)
description: Delete an Azure AD user account from PowerShell — soft-deletes the account for 30 days before permanent removal, immediately revoking sign-in access.

breakdown.meaning: Soft-delete an Azure AD user; recoverable within 30 days via the AAD recycle bin
Target user by UPN; alternatively use -ObjectId for the AAD object ID

example:
$user = Get-AzADUser -UserPrincipalName jane@contoso.com
Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken -ObjectId $user.Id
Remove-AzADUser -ObjectId $user.Id
tip: Before removing a user, revoke their active tokens with "Revoke-AzureADUserAllRefreshToken" (requires AzureAD module) to terminate live browser and app sessions immediately — Remove-AzADUser alone does not invalidate existing tokens. Document the offboarding in a runbook for audit trails.

command: Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName jane@contoso.com | Select-Object DisplayName, RoleDefinitionName, Scope
title: Get role assignments (PowerShell)
description: List all Azure RBAC role assignments for a user, service principal, or group using PowerShell — essential for access audits and diagnosing permission denied errors.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve RBAC role assignments at subscription, resource group, or resource scope
Filter to assignments for a specific user by UPN; use -ObjectId for service principals or groups
Project the three most relevant fields for a concise audit output

example: Get-AzRoleAssignment -ResourceGroupName prod-rg | Where-Object { $_.RoleDefinitionName -eq "Owner" } | Select-Object SignInName, DisplayName, Scope
output:
DisplayName    RoleDefinitionName   Scope
-----------    ------------------   -----
Jane Doe       Contributor          /subscriptions/12345678.../resourceGroups/prod-rg
Jane Doe       Reader               /subscriptions/12345678...
tip: Use Get-AzRoleAssignment -IncludeClassicAdministrators to also surface legacy Classic admin roles that are not visible in standard RBAC queries. When scoping to a resource group, inherited subscription-level assignments are also returned — filter them out with "Where-Object { $_.Scope -like "*resourceGroups*" }" if needed.

title: Assign RBAC role (PowerShell)
description: Grant an Azure RBAC role to a user, group, or service principal at subscription, resource group, or resource scope using PowerShell — the standard way to grant least-privilege access.

breakdown.meaning: Create a new RBAC role assignment binding a principal to a role at a given scope
Assign to a user by UPN; use -ObjectId for service principals or AD groups
Built-in role to assign — use the exact role name from "Get-AzRoleDefinition | Select-Object Name"
Scope the assignment to a resource group — more restrictive than subscription scope

example:
$sp = Get-AzADServicePrincipal -DisplayName "my-cicd-sp"
New-AzRoleAssignment -ObjectId $sp.Id -RoleDefinitionName "Contributor" -ResourceGroupName prod-rg
output:
RoleAssignmentId   : /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/abc123
DisplayName        : Jane Doe
RoleDefinitionName : Contributor
Scope              : /subscriptions/.../resourceGroups/my-rg
tip: Scope assignments to the smallest required resource scope — resource group is usually right for human operators, but individual resources are better for automation service principals. Avoid assigning Owner at subscription scope; use Contributor plus specific data-plane roles where needed.

title: Read / Set Key Vault secret (PowerShell)
description: Retrieve or store secrets in Azure Key Vault using PowerShell — integrates directly with SecureString and pipeline workflows to avoid plain-text secrets in scripts.

breakdown.meaning: Retrieve a secret value from Azure Key Vault
Name of the Key Vault containing the secret
Secret name within the vault
Return the secret as a plain string — omit to get a SecureString for use in credentials

example:
# Read secret as plain text
$secret = Get-AzKeyVaultSecret -VaultName my-vault -Name db-password -AsPlainText

# Set a new secret
$secureValue = ConvertTo-SecureString "newP@ssw0rd" -AsPlainText -Force
Set-AzKeyVaultSecret -VaultName my-vault -Name db-password -SecretValue $secureValue
tip: Omit -AsPlainText to keep the value as a SecureString throughout your script — pass it directly to -Password parameters of cmdlets that accept SecureString to avoid the secret ever appearing as plain text in memory or logs. Use Set-AzKeyVaultSecret to rotate secrets programmatically as part of a scheduled runbook.

command: az containerapp create --name api --resource-group myRG --image nginx:latest --target-port 80 --ingress external --environment myEnv
title: Create a Container App
description: Deploy a containerized application to Azure Container Apps — a serverless container platform that automatically scales to zero and manages the underlying infrastructure for you.

breakdown.meaning: Azure Container Apps service
Create and deploy a new container app
Name of the container app
Azure resource group to deploy into
Container image to run (Docker Hub, ACR, or any registry)
The port your container listens on
Make the app publicly accessible over HTTPS
The Container Apps environment (shared infrastructure)

flags.description: App name — also becomes part of the FQDN
Container image (include registry prefix for private registries)
external = public HTTPS endpoint; internal = accessible only within the VNet
Minimum replica count (0 = scale to zero)
Maximum replica count for autoscaling
Set environment variables for the container
Private container registry URL

example: az containerapp show --name api --resource-group myRG --query 'properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn' -o tsv
tip: Azure Container Apps automatically provisions HTTPS with a managed certificate — no cert configuration needed. Scale to zero is enabled by default, so you pay nothing when the app has no traffic. Use --min-replicas 1 to keep it warm.

command: az cosmosdb list --resource-group myRG --query '[].{Name:name, Location:location, Kind:kind}' -o table
title: List Cosmos DB accounts
description: List all Azure Cosmos DB accounts in a resource group with their locations and API kinds — Cosmos DB is a globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database service.

breakdown.meaning: Azure Cosmos DB service
Return all Cosmos DB accounts in the subscription or resource group
Filter to a specific resource group
JMESPath query to reshape output to relevant fields
Format output as a readable table

flags.description: Filter to a specific resource group
Get full details for a specific account including connection strings
Get the primary and secondary keys for an account
List SQL API databases in an account
List MongoDB API databases

example: az cosmosdb keys list --name myCosmosAccount --resource-group myRG --type keys --query primaryMasterKey -o tsv
output:
Name              Location    Kind
----------------  ----------  ----------
mycosmosaccount   eastus      GlobalDocumentDB
mymongoaccount    westus2     MongoDB
tip: Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs — GlobalDocumentDB (SQL/Core), MongoDB, Gremlin, Table, and Cassandra. The API kind is set at account creation and cannot be changed. Use az cosmosdb keys list to retrieve connection keys for your application.

command: az sql server list --resource-group myRG --query '[].{Name:name, Location:location, Admin:administratorLogin}' -o table
title: List Azure SQL servers
description: List all Azure SQL logical servers in a resource group — a logical server is the management endpoint that hosts one or more SQL databases in Azure.

breakdown.meaning: Azure SQL Server management commands
Return all SQL servers in the subscription or resource group
Filter to a specific resource group
JMESPath expression to select specific fields
Format as a readable table

flags.description: Filter to a specific resource group
List all databases on a specific SQL server

flags.flag: az sql server firewall-rule list --server NAME
flags.description: List firewall rules allowing client IP access
Get full details for a specific SQL server
Generate a connection string for a database

example: az sql db list --resource-group myRG --server my-sql-server --query '[].{Name:name, Status:status, SKU:sku.name}' -o table
output:
Name              Location    Admin
----------------  ----------  -------
my-sql-server     eastus      sqladmin
my-sql-server-2   westus2     dbadmin
tip: An Azure SQL logical server is not a VM — it is a management endpoint. The actual databases run on Microsoft-managed infrastructure. Use az sql server firewall-rule create to allow your client IP or whitelist Azure service IPs.
